name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 9 September 1967 (The Times Crossword No 1)

clue.text: Their occupation is a matter of form

definitions.text: Their occupation is a matter of form

blocks.clueFragment: Their occupation is a matter of form
blocks.note: surface reading: some job whose duties are all about etiquette and proper procedure
setter's reading: a form is a school class, and the rooms are occupied form by form

explanation.surface: Someone's profession seems to consist entirely of observing correct procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' is the British school word for a class or year group, so the occupants of these rooms are forms of pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: School teaching spaces are taken over by each class in turn, which is literally their occupation by a form.

clue.text: The bird doesn't live up to its name

definitions.text: The bird doesn't live up to its name

blocks.clueFragment: The bird doesn't live up to its name
blocks.note: surface reading: some bird whose name promises more than it delivers
setter's reading: the bird's name is also a verb for boasting or for a cockerel's call, yet this black bird only caws

explanation.surface: A disappointing bird fails to match the reputation its name suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: The black bird shares its name with the verb for exulting loudly, though its own call is a harsh caw rather than a cockerel's song.

clue.text: The source of silverside, perhaps?

blocks.note: surface reading: where a cut of beef comes from, which suggests a cow or a butcher
setter's reading: the beef cut contains silver, and the heraldic word for silver begins the answer; much beef came from that South American country

explanation.surface: A question about where a joint of silverside beef originally came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Silverside is a British cut of beef from the hindquarter. Argent is the heraldic word for silver, and the country was a great exporter of beef.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef imported from that South American nation was often of that origin, and the word also means silvery, matching the silver in silverside.

clue.text: To be out of them engenders ill feeling

definitions.text: To be out of them engenders ill feeling

blocks.clueFragment: To be out of them engenders ill feeling
blocks.note: surface reading: running short of something leaves people resentful
setter's reading: completes the idiom for being slightly unwell or grumpy

explanation.surface: Running out of some supply breeds resentment among people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill feeling' looks like hostility between people, but it means feeling unwell, as in the idiom 'out of sorts'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'out of sorts' describes a person who is mildly unwell or irritable, so lacking these produces that state.

clue.text: An initial change in this direction would cause a mishap

blocks.note: setter's reading: alter only the first letter of the answer
swapping the opening O for an A yields the ordinary word for a mishap

explanation.surface: A small early change of course in some direction leads to a mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the first letter from O to A and the compass word turns into ACCIDENT, a mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: The occident is the west, the direction of the setting sun, so it names a compass direction.

clue.text: Solo lamentation

blocks.note: surface reading: a person grieving alone
setter's reading: a poem or ode for a single voice, in Greek tradition a mournful one

explanation.definitionFit: A monody is an ode sung by one voice in Greek tragedy, and by extension an elegy or poem mourning a death.

clue.text: National transport publicity has point

blocks.note: BR is British Rail, the old nationalised railway
an ad is an advertisement, a piece of publicity

explanation.surface: The state railway's advertising campaign makes a valid point.
explanation.walkthrough: BR stood for British Rail, Britain's state-owned railway when this was set.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a thin small-headed nail, something with a sharp tip used for fixing.

clue.text: Game birds when cornered

blocks.note: surface reading: hunted fowl trapped with no escape
setter's reading: the game is chess, whose castles stand in the board's corners at the start and share a name with black birds

explanation.surface: Hunted fowl find themselves trapped in a corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game birds' suggests pheasant or grouse, but the game is chess.
explanation.definitionFit: The chess castles begin in the four corners of the board and are named like the black crow-family birds.

clue.text: All to pieces, like Elijah in translation?

blocks.note: surface reading: completely broken apart
setter's reading: when the prophet was taken up to heaven his cloak fell from him, so he lost his mantle

explanation.surface: Something has fallen apart, as the prophet Elijah did when carried off.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible Elijah is 'translated', carried bodily to heaven, and his mantle falls to Elisha; so he was dis-mantled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taken apart into its components is in pieces, and read as two parts the word means stripped of a cloak.

clue.text: A. Selkirk was, in a monarchical sense, according to Cowper

definitions.text: A. Selkirk was, in a monarchical sense, according to Cowper

blocks.clueFragment: A. Selkirk was, in a monarchical sense, according to Cowper
blocks.note: surface reading: a historical note on a castaway's status
setter's reading: Cowper's poem has the castaway say 'I am monarch of all I survey'

explanation.surface: A literary note about the castaway Alexander Selkirk as portrayed by the poet Cowper.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Selkirk, the model for Robinson Crusoe, is the speaker of Cowper's verses beginning 'I am monarch of all I survey'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who looks over land is one who surveys it, and the poem crowns Selkirk king of everything he views.

clue.text: No rag can disrupt this place

indicators.note: to disrupt is to throw into disorder, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

blocks.note: the five letters taken as written

explanation.surface: No student rag week could disturb the peace of this quiet place.
explanation.walkthrough: Ongar is a small town in Essex; a rag is a British student charity stunt.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a market town in Essex, England, so it is fairly called a place.

clue.text: The empty - sleeved fraternity?

blocks.note: surface reading: a group of amputees or of people with tucked-up sleeves
setter's reading: stage magicians insist they have nothing up their sleeves

explanation.surface: A brotherhood defined by sleeves with nothing in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage magicians famously show there is nothing hidden up their sleeves before performing tricks, making them a sleeve-empty brotherhood.

clue.text: Partial like the partially developed street

blocks.note: first meaning: biased, favouring one party
second meaning: a road with houses built along only one of its edges

explanation.surface: Something is biased, like a street only half built up.
explanation.definitionFit: A biased view favours one party, and a road with buildings along just one edge is literally so.

clue.text: She should be a match for anyone

definitions.text: She should be a match for anyone

blocks.clueFragment: She should be a match for anyone
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman equal to any opponent
setter's reading: the Roman hearth goddess gave her name to a brand of wax matches

explanation.surface: A formidable woman who could take on all comers.
explanation.walkthrough: Vestas were short wax matches, named after the Roman goddess of the hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of hearth and fire is female and lent her name to a well-known make of matches.

clue.text: A fan from the USA isn't!

indicators.note: the answer is made out of the following words, their letters rearranged to form it

blocks.note: all ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A jibe that a keen supporter does not come from America.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark points to the joke: the letters of 'the USA isn't' really are the source.
explanation.definitionFit: An avid supporter or devotee of something is called a fan, short for fanatic.

clue.text: Showing some disapprobation from the stalls?

definitions.text: Showing some disapprobation from the stalls?

blocks.clueFragment: Showing some disapprobation from the stalls?
blocks.note: surface reading: a theatre audience in the cheaper seats booing
setter's reading: stable stalls hold horses, whose call can sound like a jeer

explanation.surface: Theatregoers in the stalls voice their displeasure at a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Horses kept in a stable call out with a high whinny, which sounds like a scornful 'nay'.

clue.text: Painfully conspicuous by its absence in the Nut-cracker Suite?

definitions.text: Painfully conspicuous by its absence in the Nut-cracker Suite?

blocks.clueFragment: Painfully conspicuous by its absence in the Nut-cracker Suite?
blocks.note: surface reading: something missing from Tchaikovsky's ballet music
setter's reading: a suite of rooms where the nut, slang for the skull, keeps getting banged on a low ceiling

explanation.surface: Something noticeably missing from Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker Suite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' is slang for head, and a suite can be a set of rooms; a nut-cracker suite is one where you hit your head.
explanation.definitionFit: The clearance between your crown and the ceiling is the space you need to stand upright without injury.

clue.text: One product of the pen

blocks.note: surface reading: something written, a piece of writing
setter's reading: a pen is a female swan, whose young is a baby swan

explanation.surface: A single piece of writing produced by a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A female swan is called a pen, and the young bird she hatches is a baby swan.

clue.text: Suitable sub-title for "A Woman of No Importance"?

definitions.text: Suitable sub-title for "A Woman of No Importance"?

blocks.clueFragment: Suitable sub-title for "A Woman of No Importance"?
blocks.note: surface reading: an alternative heading for Oscar Wilde's play
setter's reading: a person of no importance is a cipher, a nobody

explanation.surface: Suggesting a second title for Oscar Wilde's play about a disregarded woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who counts for nothing is an insignificant person, exactly what Wilde's title describes.

clue.text: Champion description of a dirty carpet

blocks.note: first meaning: never defeated, as a title-holder may be
second meaning: a rug that has not had the dust thrashed out of it

explanation.surface: A splendid way to describe a grubby rug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion' reads as an adjective meaning excellent, but stands for a winner never defeated.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion who has never lost is undefeated, and a rug never thrashed with a carpet-beater remains dusty.

clue.text: Sources of wild laughter

blocks.note: surface reading: things that make people laugh uncontrollably
setter's reading: African wild animals whose cry sounds like cackling laughter

explanation.surface: Things that set people off into hysterical laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: These African scavenging animals are known for a cackling call that sounds like human laughing.

clue.text: Charm common to some schools

blocks.note: first meaning: as a verb, to delight or bewitch
second meaning: Common ... is the exam for admission to British independent schools

explanation.surface: A quality of charm shared by certain schools.
explanation.walkthrough: Common Entrance is the exam British children sit to get into fee-paying senior schools; 'common' is part of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewitch or enchant someone is to entrance them, and admission tests for schools are entrance exams.

clue.text: "Or emptied some d ill - to the drains" (Keats)

definitions.text: "Or emptied some d ill - to the drains" (Keats)

blocks.clueFragment: "Or emptied some d ill - to the drains" (Keats)
blocks.note: surface reading: a line from Keats with a word missing
setter's reading: the gap is filled from the Ode to a Nightingale, 'or emptied some dull ___ to the drains'

explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'd ill' is the word 'dull'; the missing word completes the second line of Keats's Ode to a Nightingale.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem the speaker feels as if he has drunk a narcotic drug, emptying it to the dregs.

clue.text: The first part of a girl's make-up

definitions.text: The first part of a girl's make-up

blocks.clueFragment: The first part of a girl's make-up
blocks.note: surface reading: the foundation or first cosmetic a girl applies
setter's reading: make-up means composition, and the nursery rhyme lists what little girls are made of, a sweetener first

explanation.surface: The first cosmetic a girl puts on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' suggests cosmetics but means composition, as in the rhyme 'What are little girls made of?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme lists the sweet ingredient first among what little girls are made of, before spice.

clue.text: Dress for the rising generation?

blocks.note: surface reading: clothes for young people on the way up
setter's reading: what you do when rising from bed, which also names an outfit

explanation.surface: Fashion aimed at the up-and-coming young.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfit or costume is informally a get-up, and the phrasal verb for leaving your bed is the same.

clue.text: At Nap he's uncommonly game

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests things out of their usual order, so the letters are shuffled

blocks.note: taken as written
the S of he's

explanation.surface: At the card game Nap, he's unusually brave.
explanation.walkthrough: Nap is a card game; 'game' looks like 'plucky' but names a hunted bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-tailed bird is shot for sport and food, so it is classic game in the hunting sense.

clue.text: Man's episcopal associate

blocks.note: surface reading: a bishop's assistant or chaplain
setter's reading: the Isle of Man, paired with another name in its bishop's title

explanation.surface: A bishop's companion or aide.
explanation.walkthrough: The Church of England diocese covering the Isle of Man is 'Sodor and Man', so its bishop's title links the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man's bishopric is styled Sodor and Man, so this name is joined to Man in church usage.

clue.text: Sound, but dangerous for pussy

blocks.note: first meaning: healthy, in good shape
second meaning: in the nursery rhyme 'Ding dong bell, pussy's in the' shaft for drawing water

explanation.surface: Something safe enough, yet a hazard for a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in good health is described this way, and a deep shaft for water is where the rhyme's cat fell.

clue.text: He has no trouble losing weight

definitions.text: He has no trouble losing weight

blocks.clueFragment: He has no trouble losing weight
blocks.note: surface reading: a man who slims easily
setter's reading: in orbit a space traveller becomes weightless

explanation.surface: A man for whom dieting comes easily.
explanation.definitionFit: A space traveller in orbit experiences weightlessness, losing all apparent heaviness without any dieting.

clue.text: What one displays in learning to do it makes nonsense of it

definitions.text: What one displays in learning to do it makes nonsense of it

blocks.clueFragment: What one displays in learning to do it
blocks.note: surface reading: a quality shown by a learner, such as energy or determination
setter's reading: a learner at the wheel shows the opposite of skill at operating a car, so the word is mocked

explanation.surface: A paradox about a quality a learner shows that undermines the very task.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both energetic determination and steering a car; a learner shows determination but not competent steering.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both energy and ambition, which a learner displays, and operating a motor car, which is being learnt.

clue.text: Specimen from the composing room

blocks.note: first meaning: an example or representative of a class
second meaning: the metal letters a printer's compositor sets

explanation.surface: A sample taken from where printers set pages.
explanation.definitionFit: A representative example is one model of a kind, and printers' metal letters set by compositors share the name.

clue.text: This kind of mint produces a coin fit for a king

blocks.note: a penny is a small coin
royal means befitting a monarch

explanation.surface: A mint turns out a coin worthy of a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' looks like the place that strikes coins, but it is the herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennyroyal is a small European herb of the mint family, once used medicinally.
